nature-found-096.title: Humanity's demand on the biosphere versus its regeneration
nature-found-096.text:
The Dasgupta Review reduces the whole sustainability question to a comparison. On one side is humanity's demand for the biosphere's goods and services. On the other is the rate at which the biosphere regenerates. When demand exceeds regeneration, the biosphere depreciates.

The framing builds on Ehrlich and Holdren's 1971 split of impact into population, individual demands and the technologies and institutions in play. Their impact, humanity's demand per unit of time, is today known as the global ecological footprint. Demand takes two forms: harvesting goods and services for consumption and production, and using the biosphere as a sink for waste.

Both extraction X and waste Z grow with population times income per capita, divided by efficiency terms: X = Ny/alpha_X and Z = Ny/alpha_Z. Income stands in for human activity, though it almost surely understates it. Over the long run, demand must equal what the biosphere can sustainably supply, and uncovering that relation is the core of the Review.

nature-found-091.title: Produced, human and natural capital: three kinds of wealth
nature-found-091.text:
Roads and patents, skills and a sea view: the Dasgupta Review sorts all of them into three kinds of capital goods. The word capital has not always been so generous. Economists confine it to assets that are measurable, and the range has widened over time.

Roads, buildings, machines, ports and patents are tangible or intangible but alienable, meaning they can be sold on. Together they are called produced capital. Health, education and skills are intangible and cannot be handed to someone else. They form human capital, which entered the list once ways were found to measure its value to individuals and society.

Natural capital, introduced earlier as {{ref:nature-found-010}}, became the third category once methods existed to measure the value people place on natural resources. It runs from plants, which are tangible and alienable, to pollinators, a sea view and the global climate, which are intangible and not alienable.

The Review stresses a wedge between market prices of capital goods, especially natural capital, and their accounting or shadow prices. A shadow price is the contribution an extra unit makes to the flow of social benefits. Many kinds of natural capital have no market and are free to the user, so special methods are needed to estimate it. Mainstream growth and development theories, and the models used by finance ministries and central banks, leave out humanity's dependence on Nature.

nature-found-093.title: Why Nature does not maximise productivity
nature-found-093.text:
A portfolio manager would chase the highest yield. Nature does not. It maximises neither net primary production (NPP), the plant growth that feeds ecosystems, nor the regeneration rate of its ecosystems.

NPP per square metre differs by biome: 0.75 kg a year in temperate grassland, 2.5 in tropical rainforest and 0.14 in the ocean, because the abiotic environment varies. Even after allowing for that, planetary NPP is not at its maximum, and NPP in old growth forests is nearly zero. Life-form distributions emerged under selection pressures at the genetic level, not as an efficient spread of NPP. In the Review's fishery example, yield is zero at the long-run population K, so the marginal product of the fish stock there is negative.

nature-found-097.title: Impact inequality: unequal incomes, unequal footprints
nature-found-097.text:
Two households with the same income can press on the biosphere very differently. The Dasgupta Review therefore separates inequality in household incomes from inequality in impact, which is income corrected for the efficiency of converting nature into income.

Households differ in both income and that efficiency. A household's income divided by its efficiency (y/alpha) can be read as its ecological footprint, the demand idea from {{ref:nature-found-096}}. Across 136 countries the Review estimates footprint I = 0.97 y^0.41, where y is income per capita. One consequence follows: the global ecological footprint would be higher than today's if everyone received an equal share of today's global income.

nature-found-094.title: Regulating services work unseen until they fail
nature-found-094.text:
Mangroves yield visible timber and fish. Their protection of villages against storms is appreciated only after they are degraded, and it is far harder to value. That is the problem with regulating and maintenance services, the kind described in {{ref:nature-found-007}}: they are mostly hidden and silent, felt only over the long run or when they are lost.

Provisioning and cultural services are different, since their outcomes are readily detected even in the short run. A study of the 1999 Orissa super-cyclone found that villages protected by more mangroves suffered less property damage. The social cost of shrimp, then, should include the carbon sequestered by the mangroves cleared for shrimp farms and the protection they gave nearby communities.

nature-found-095.title: Why Nature's mobility and silence breed externalities
nature-found-095.text:
No one can contain the air they foul or the rivers they pollute. Externalities arise from the biosphere because property rights to large parts of it are weakly defined or enforced, and because Nature is mobile, silent and invisible.

An externality is an unaccounted-for consequence of one person's actions for others, including future people. The harm from fouled air or water is non-excludable. Nitrogen and phosphorus in an estuary aggregate leakages from innumerable distant fields, factories and households, so polluters do not pay for using it as a sink. No property rights cover the oceans beyond national jurisdiction, so no one has an incentive to protect them from contamination or overfishing.

Public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, a mirror image of open access resources. They are underproduced for the same reason that open access resources are overused.

nature-found-092.title: An asset's own rate of return
nature-found-092.text:
How much is one more unit of an asset worth tomorrow? The answer is its yield, or own rate of return: the growth expected tomorrow if one more unit is added to a portfolio today.

For produced capital, yield is its marginal product. For a fishery or a tree, it is the growth in biomass obtained by waiting. Investment can therefore be passive: restoring a wetland is investment, and so is conservation, which can simply mean waiting. Applied to {{ref:nature-found-010}}, the idea lets nature be compared with other assets.

Yield is a pure number per unit of time. The UK government's long-term bonds have historically averaged about 4% a year, though more recently closer to 1%. Because relative prices change unless the economy is stationary, own rates are not enough: the rate of return on an asset is its yield plus its capital gains over a unit of time.

nature-found-101.title: Risk assessment: weighing hazards by likelihood and loss
nature-found-101.text:
A risk assessment asks what could go wrong, how likely it is and what could be done about it. It is a process for identifying hazards and the likelihood they occur, and the actions that can reduce their harmful effects.

It can be done at the scale of an individual or of a whole system such as an ecosystem or a hurricane. Non-linear complex systems are harder to assess. In quantitative work, annualized loss expectancy is the single loss expectancy times the annualized rate of occurrence.

Acceptable risk is one tolerated because the cost of a countermeasure exceeds the expected loss. Public health often uses a lifetime risk increase of one in a million. Its assessments characterize the nature and likelihood of harm to people from human activities, and facilities may be barred unless risk stays below a threshold.

nature-found-040.title: Environmental valuation: pricing what has no price
nature-found-040.text:
When natural assets go unpriced, they tend to be both overused and underinvested in. Environmental valuation tries to fix that by putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price. It draws on {{ref:nature-found-030}}, and it is one way to put numbers on {{ref:nature-found-010}} and on the harms described in {{ref:nature-found-031}}.

Use values can be read from behaviour, such as the cost of recreational trips or house prices in hedonic methods. Non-use values include existence value, option value and bequest value, such as wanting to leave a pristine environment to one's children. These are usually estimated with surveys such as contingent valuation or choice modelling. Contingent valuation asks people what they would pay for an environmental good, or accept for its loss.

The stakes are practical. Without dollar values for benefits such as clean air and water, estimates of pollution-control benefits fall below true social benefits and policy chronically underinvests.

Valuation is controversial. Some environmentalists object to pricing what may be priceless, though such values keep society from ignoring nature in policy choices. Willingness to pay is budget constrained and tends to be lower where incomes are lower, raising equity problems. Willingness to accept is not constrained and can in theory approach infinity.

nature-found-103.title: Biodiversity risk assessment: species and ecosystems at risk
nature-found-103.text: This is {{ref:nature-found-101}} applied to living diversity, with species extinction or ecosystem collapse as the outcomes of concern. The units assessed are biological, such as species and populations, or ecological, such as habitats and ecosystems. Risks often relate to human threats and pressures. The IUCN Red List of Ecosystems was developed for biodiversity risk assessment, with collapse as the most extreme outcome.

nature-found-102.title: Environmental risk assessment of stressors
nature-found-102.text: Environmental risk assessment applies {{ref:nature-found-101}} to the effects of stressors, usually chemicals, on the local environment. Risk here is an integrated assessment of the likelihood and severity of an undesired event. The likelihood of harm and its size are judged together, not separately.

nature-found-098.title: Persistent organic pollutants: chemicals that will not break down
nature-found-098.text:
Some chemicals released decades ago are still circulating in bodies and food webs. Persistent organic pollutants, or POPs, are organic compounds that resist chemical, biological and photolytic degradation and are toxic to health and the environment. They are a hard case of the {{ref:nature-found-075}} and of {{ref:nature-found-055}}.

Most POPs are man-made pesticides or insecticides, plus some solvents, pharmaceuticals and industrial chemicals. A few arise naturally from volcanoes and forest fires. They harm the environment through long-range transport and bioaccumulation, which reconcentrates them to potentially dangerous levels.

Being halogenated and lipid soluble, they accumulate in fatty tissue, and concentrations rise up the food chain as biomagnification. Because wind and water carry them, POPs released in one country affect people and wildlife far away, including the Antarctic and the Arctic. For people not exposed through accident or work, over 90% of exposure comes from animal-product foods.

nature-found-099.title: The Stockholm Convention bans the dirty dozen
nature-found-099.text:
On May 22, 2001, governments adopted an agreement under the UN Environment Programme to protect human health and the environment from {{ref:nature-found-098}}. As of 2024, 185 countries plus the European Union had ratified it.

It initially listed twelve POPs, banning them and requiring parties to eliminate or reduce their release. The 'dirty dozen' include DDT, PCBs and dioxins. The list has since grown to include some PAHs, brominated flame retardants and other compounds, and chlorpyrifos was added in 2025. Because these compounds travel on wind and water, an agreement among many countries suits a problem that a single country cannot contain, much like the wider problem of {{ref:nature-found-055}}.

nature-found-104.title: Smog: when smoke meets fog
nature-found-104.text:
Smog, or smoke fog, is a type of intense air pollution. The word is a portmanteau of smoke and fog, first used for London's pea soup fog. Coinage is credited to Henry Antoine Des Voeux in 1905, though it appeared in print in 1880.

Coal fires, which have caused air pollution in England since the Middle Ages, and traffic emissions of carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds are main human causes. Eruptions give a natural volcanic smog called vog, and plant hydrocarbons such as isoprene and terpenes can be more reactive than man-made ones.

Smog precursors can be carried downwind, so episodes can hit regions far from emission sources. About 35 to 60% of Beijing's ozone comes from outside the city. Basins such as Los Angeles, Mexico City and Santiago trap pollution. The costs are concrete: Ontario sustains an estimated $201 million in annual damages to selected crops, and Vancouver loses an estimated $7.5 million in tourism revenue to reduced visibility.

nature-found-100.title: How persistent organic pollutants harm health
nature-found-100.text: The harms of exposure to POPs include developmental defects, chronic illness, endocrine disruption and cancer risk. Timing matters: low-level exposure in critical developmental periods can permanently change development, while exposure outside them may show no later disease. Mixtures of POPs are assumed additive but can be synergistic, exceeding the approximated additive effect. Indoor air and dust POP levels often exceed outdoor levels, which challenges the view that food is the main route.

nature-found-106.title: What smog does to human health
nature-found-106.text: Smog continues to harm human health in many cities. Ontario's medical association estimated that it causes about 9,500 premature deaths a year in the province. A 20-year American Cancer Society study found that cumulative exposure raises premature respiratory death, implying the 8-hour standard may be insufficient. In 2016 a Lancet study linked a 5 microgram change in PM2.5 to an 18% higher risk of low birth weight, even below accepted safe levels. Haze and smoke also cut irradiance, hurting solar photovoltaic output and agricultural yield.

nature-found-105.title: Photochemical smog: sunlight turns exhaust into ozone
nature-found-105.text: Summer smog forms when sunlight reacts with nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, leaving particles and ground-level ozone. Sunlight splits nitrogen dioxide into nitric oxide and an oxygen atom that forms ozone. VOCs react with the nitric oxide, so ozone is not removed and builds up with peroxyacetyl nitrates. These secondary pollutants, ozone, PANs and aldehydes, irritate eyes and airways and reduce lung function, particularly in sensitive people.

nature-found-107.title: Soundscape ecology: listening to ecosystems
nature-found-107.text:
Soundscape ecology studies the acoustic relationships between living organisms, human and other, and their environment. Soundscapes combine biophony from organisms, geophony from natural non-biological sources and anthropophony from humans.

Anthropogenic noise, the subject of {{ref:nature-found-067}}, masks acoustic signals, harming communication, foraging and predator recognition across fish, amphibians, birds and mammals. Great tits in noisy urban territories sing at higher frequencies and with shorter, faster-repeated songs. Noise can reduce insect diversity and abundance, with possible knock-on effects on ecosystem services such as pollination. Natural soundscapes are now a conservation goal and may be considered ecosystem services provided by intact ecosystems.

nature-econ-095.title: Opportunity cost: the price of the road not taken
nature-econ-095.text:
A government that spends $840 billion on a war cannot also spend it on healthcare, education or tax cuts. That forgone alternative is the heart of opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up when limited resources force you to pick one option over others. It is the benefit you would have had from the second-best choice.

The idea expresses the link between {{ref:nature-found-051}} and choice, and its aim is efficient use of scarce resources. It counts all costs of a decision, explicit and implicit, and is not limited to money. Lost time, pleasure or any useful benefit also counts. Suppose someone leaves work for an hour to spend $200 on office supplies and earns $25 an hour. The $200 is the explicit cost and the $25 of lost earnings the implicit cost.

Sunk costs, already spent and unrecoverable, are excluded and should not sway present or future decisions. Every {{ref:nature-econ-099}} carries an opportunity cost, and a party that can produce something at a lower opportunity cost than others has a comparative advantage in it.

Nature conservation shows the same logic. Endangered species protection carries opportunity costs such as old-growth timber that cannot be cut and urban habitat that cannot be built on.

nature-econ-848.title: Capitalism: private property run for profit
nature-econ-848.text:
Capitalism is an economic system built on private ownership of the means of production, run to obtain profit. Its constituent elements are private property, profit motive, capital accumulation, competitive markets, commodification, wage labor, and an emphasis on innovation and economic growth.

Capital accumulation is central: financial capital, as in {{ref:nature-econ-083}}, is invested for profit, then reinvested in further production in a continuous process. Economic growth is a characteristic tendency of capitalist economies, which also swing through business cycles of expansion and recession.

There is no universally agreed definition, and it is unclear whether capitalism describes a whole society or only elements of one. Green variants exist. Eco-capitalism holds that natural capital, ecosystems with ecological yield, underlies all wealth, so governments should use market instruments such as a carbon tax against environmental problems. Sustainable capitalism is a conceptual form built on sustainable practices that reduce externalities, though one account notes that a capitalist economy must expand to survive and find new markets.

nature-econ-849.title: Planned economy: allocation by economy-wide plan
nature-econ-849.text:
In a planned economy, investment, production and the allocation of capital goods, as in {{ref:nature-econ-083}}, follow economy-wide plans. Planning can be centralized, decentralized, participatory or Soviet-type. It contrasts with market economies, where autonomous firms decide production, pricing and investment. Market economies using indicative planning are called mixed economies or planned market economies.

Critics argue planners cannot detect consumer preferences, shortages and surpluses accurately enough. Mises and Hayek described this as the economic calculation problem and the local knowledge problem. Supporters argue the state can direct land, labor and capital to its objectives. In the 1930s Soviet Union, private consumption was forced down from 80% to 50% of gross national income.
